newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croats await official word on Tudjman's illness.
newsitem.headline: Croats await official word on Tudjman's illness.

text.p: Many Croats refused to believe on Saturday that President Franjo Tudjman, identified with the country's fight for independence, was seriously ill.
United States officials said on Friday the 74-year old Croatian president had stomach cancer and was undergoing treatment at a Washington hospital.
But strictly-controlled state television in Croatia played down the illness, saying Tudjman was flown to the United States for treatment following some "digestion problems".
A group of opposition politicians lashed out at the state media on Saturday, saying it operated in the same way as in the "old days" -- when Croatia was part of communist Yugoslavia.
"The public has a right to know the truth, and not to be manipulated by the state-run media like this," said former Croatian Foreign Minister Zvonimir Separovic.
Leading Croatian newspapers on Saturday ignored the public's thirst for knowledge about the president's condition.

Of the three main dailies, two had nothing but short agency reports and one had a second-page spread with details about the Walter Reed hospital, where Tudjman is being treated, and all of its modern equipment.
Zdravko Pavelic, an elderly physician, put his trust in the state media and believed Tudjman's health was not in jeopardy.

"The radio said he had a stomach ulcer, and that is not an incurable disease," said Pavelic, sitting in a cafe on the main Zagreb square. "We hope that it is not a grave disease and that he will get better," said his companion.
Some of Tudjman's supporters thought it inappropriate that the Western media should openly discuss the president's health.
"That's not true, do not spread lies. I am his neighbour and I forbid you to tell such awful things about him," said a woman in her sixties on her way to the outdoor market.
Among those who had a chance to see foreign media reports, there was deep concern for the country's future stability.

"I think this could affect the political situation in Croatia. It could turn for the worse...I think he has done quite a lot for Croatia and if someone else comes, I don't know what would happen," said a young woman selling newspapers.
An official government announcement that Tudjman was in hospital came only after U.S. media broke the story.
For several hours, a senior Croatian embassy official in Washington denied that Tudjman was in the city.
